title: Installing ansible-core
shortDescription: Build and verify an Ansible control node on RHEL 9.
description: Register RHEL, inspect subscribed repositories, install the RHEL-provided ansible-core RPM, and prove that Ansible can execute a module.
coverAlt: RHEL terminal showing the installed ansible-core package and Ansible version
outcomes: Connect RHEL to Red Hat services
Install and inspect the RHEL-provided ansible-core RPM
Validate a working Ansible control node

prerequisites.label: System
prerequisites.detail: A current RHEL 9 physical or virtual machine.

prerequisites.label: Access
prerequisites.detail: A user that can run administrative commands with sudo.

prerequisites.label: Connectivity
prerequisites.detail: Outbound access to Red Hat registration and content services.

prerequisites.label: Subscription
prerequisites.detail: A RHEL entitlement provides the BaseOS and AppStream access needed to install this RPM. An Ansible Automation Platform subscription is not required for the lab, but a RHEL subscription does not provide broad support for arbitrary ansible-core automation.

comparisons.title: RHEL 9 AppStream ansible-core vs upstream ansible-core
comparisons.introduction: These are not different automation engines: both provide the ansible-core command-line tools, language, extensible runtime, and ansible.builtin content. The RHEL RPM is Red Hat's downstream build of the upstream project. The important differences are packaging, version policy, update authority, lifecycle, and support scope. Package access through a RHEL subscription must not be confused with blanket support for every ansible-core use case.

values: Provides the ansible-core CLI, playbook language, runtime framework, and built-in ansible.builtin modules and plugins as integrated into RHEL.
Provides the same categories of core CLI tools, playbook language, runtime framework, and ansible.builtin modules and plugins directly from the upstream project.
A Red Hat-built, signed, and tested RPM derived from upstream source and delivered through the RHEL AppStream repository.
A release produced from the ansible/ansible stable branch, published as an upstream Python distribution and identified by its X.Y.Z version.
Install and update with DNF. RPM tracks ownership, dependencies, signatures, and errata with the rest of the operating system.
Install into a selected Python environment with pip or into an isolated application environment with pipx. That environment's Python packaging workflow owns upgrades and dependencies.
Uses the RHEL filesystem layout and platform Python dependencies; commands are installed system-wide under RPM control.
Location and Python runtime depend on the interpreter, user site, virtual environment, or pipx environment selected during installation.
RHEL 9 stays on the ansible-core 2.14 stream and advances the RPM release when Red Hat delivers fixes. A lower upstream version number does not by itself mean the RPM is unpatched.
A new X.Y feature release normally arrives about every six months, with X.Y.Z servicing releases on an approximately four-week schedule.
The RHEL product lifecycle and AppStream policy govern maintenance; upstream end-of-life alone does not determine the status of the RHEL RPM.

The project maintains three feature releases at graduated levels: the newest receives general bug and security fixes, the next receives critical and security fixes, and the oldest receives security fixes.
Red Hat can backport selected fixes to the retained version to reduce compatibility risk. Use Red Hat advisories and security data—not only the upstream version string—to assess the RPM.
Fixes are backported among maintained stable branches according to severity and appear in new upstream servicing releases; unmaintained releases generally stop receiving fixes.
Red Hat lists ansible-core 2.14 as a Full Life Application Stream for RHEL 9, aligning the stream with the underlying RHEL major-release lifecycle and applicable errata policy.
Lifecycle follows the upstream support matrix and changes as each new feature release moves the previous releases into narrower maintenance phases and eventually end of life.

RHEL support is deliberately limited to playbooks, roles, or modules supplied by or generated by Red Hat products, including RHEL System Roles and Red Hat Insights-generated automation. Broader support for the core platform and core-maintained modules requires Ansible Automation Platform.
The upstream project provides documentation, maintenance releases, issue tracking, and community collaboration, but installing its release does not create a Red Hat product-support entitlement.
Prioritizes RHEL integration, predictable package management, and a stable feature baseline while selected fixes arrive as RPM updates.

Makes newer core behavior, Python support, and features available sooner; feature-release upgrades can require porting work because ansible-core does not promise complete compatibility between X.Y releases.
The RPM supplies ansible-core and ansible.builtin. Install any additional collections required by your automation from an appropriate trusted source and manage their own versions and support status.
The upstream release likewise supplies ansible-core and ansible.builtin. Additional collections are selected, installed, upgraded, and supported separately from the core runtime.

comparisons.takeaway: For this RHEL 9 lab, use the AppStream RPM because it is integrated with DNF and the RHEL lifecycle. Choose an upstream ansible-core release when you specifically need a newer core feature or Python compatibility and are prepared to own the Python environment, upgrade cadence, regression testing, and upstream project support path. If you need Red Hat support for general-purpose automation rather than only Red Hat-supplied or generated content, evaluate an Ansible Automation Platform subscription; installing the RHEL RPM alone does not expand the RHEL support scope.

steps.label: Verify
steps.title: Verify the RHEL 9 starting environment
steps.alt: Clean Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 desktop with a terminal ready for commands
steps.explanation: Confirm the operating system, processor architecture, hostname, and clean package state before making changes. This recording uses RHEL 9 on aarch64; your architecture and hostname may differ.
steps.expected: The host reports RHEL 9, a supported architecture, its own hostname, and that ansible-core is not installed.
steps.note: The demonstration VM was fully upgraded before recording. On an existing system, rpm may report an installed package; compare its version before continuing.
steps.troubleshooting: If the system is not RHEL 9, stop and use installation guidance for that operating system. If ansible-core is already installed, this lab can still be used to inspect and verify it.

steps.label: Register
steps.title: Connect the system to Red Hat
steps.alt: RHEL terminal confirming successful connections to Red Hat Subscription Management and Insights
steps.explanation: The rhc client prompts interactively for your Red Hat account and connects the host to Subscription Management and Insights. Enter credentials only at those prompts—never place them in a command, recording, transcript, or script.
steps.expected: rhc reports successful connections to Red Hat Subscription Management and Insights and activates remote host configuration.
steps.note: Credential input is excluded from the replay. The neutral placeholders show where learners interact without exposing an account name or password.
steps.troubleshooting: If no credential prompt appears, make sure rhc connect is running in an interactive terminal. If registration fails, verify network, DNS, proxy, system time, and the account's RHEL entitlement.

steps.label: Confirm
steps.title: Confirm the Red Hat connections
steps.alt: RHEL terminal showing active Subscription Management and Red Hat Insights connections
steps.explanation: Verify the result independently after rhc connect finishes. The two service connection lines confirm that the host can obtain subscribed content and report to Insights.
steps.expected: The system is connected to Red Hat Subscription Management and Red Hat Insights.
steps.note: The remote host configuration daemon may later report inactive. That optional daemon state does not prevent DNF from installing ansible-core from subscribed repositories.
steps.troubleshooting: If either required connection is unavailable, retry rhc connect and review network, DNS, proxy, time synchronization, and entitlement access before continuing.

steps.label: Repositories
steps.title: Verify the enabled repositories
steps.alt: DNF output listing enabled RHEL BaseOS and AppStream repositories
steps.command:
sudo subscription-manager repos --list-enabled
sudo dnf repolist --enabled
steps.explanation: subscription-manager shows the repositories enabled in the Red Hat subscription configuration. dnf repolist shows the enabled repositories DNF can currently use. BaseOS supplies the operating-system foundation; AppStream contains ansible-core and several dependencies.
steps.expected: Both the RHEL 9 BaseOS and AppStream RPM repositories appear as enabled.
steps.note: Repository IDs include the architecture. This recording uses aarch64; x86_64 systems show corresponding x86_64 repository IDs.
steps.troubleshooting: If either repository is missing, refresh subscription data, then enable the architecture-specific BaseOS and AppStream repository IDs shown in the troubleshooting guide.

steps.label: Inspect
steps.title: Inspect the RHEL-provided package
steps.alt: DNF repoquery output showing ansible-core package information
steps.explanation: Inspecting the package before installation confirms its version, architecture, source repository, size, license, and purpose. The exact version will change as Red Hat publishes updates.
steps.expected: The latest ansible-core build is available from the RHEL 9 AppStream repository.
steps.troubleshooting: If DNF reports no matching package, verify that AppStream is enabled, clean the DNF metadata, and rebuild the cache.

steps.label: Install
steps.title: Install ansible-core with DNF
steps.alt: DNF transaction completing the ansible-core installation
steps.explanation: DNF resolves and installs ansible-core plus required Python, SSH, and Git dependencies. Review the transaction summary before confirming the installation in your environment.
steps.expected: The transaction finishes with Complete! and lists ansible-core among the installed packages.
steps.troubleshooting: If dependency resolution fails, refresh package metadata and review the transaction without disabling signature checks or forcing package removal.

steps.label: Validate
steps.title: Confirm the package and runtime
steps.alt: Terminal output showing the ansible-core RPM and Ansible version details
steps.command:
rpm -q ansible-core
rpm -V ansible-core && echo "Package verification: passed"
dnf list --installed ansible-core
command -v ansible
command -v ansible-playbook
ansible --version
steps.explanation: Confirm the installed RPM, verify that its packaged files are unchanged, locate both primary command-line tools, and inspect the runtime. The version output identifies the active configuration file, Python runtime, module paths, and collection paths.
steps.expected: All commands return successfully and ansible --version reports the installed core release.
steps.troubleshooting: If rpm -V prints file differences, investigate them before relying on the installation. If the shell cannot find ansible, start a new terminal or run hash -r, then check /usr/bin/ansible.

steps.label: Explore
steps.title: Inspect configuration and module help
steps.alt: Terminal showing Ansible configuration and ping module documentation
steps.command:
PAGER=cat ansible-config dump --only-changed
PAGER=cat ansible-doc -s ansible.builtin.ping
steps.explanation: PAGER=cat sets the pager only for the command that follows, so output is written directly to the terminal instead of opening an interactive viewer such as less. ansible-config dump prints Ansible's resolved configuration, and --only-changed limits the result to values that differ from built-in defaults. The second command confirms that built-in module documentation is available; ansible.builtin.ping is the module's fully qualified collection name.
steps.expected: Ansible shows the active configuration file or other settings that differ from defaults, then displays the argument summary for ansible.builtin.ping. On a system with no changed settings, the first command can legitimately produce little or no output.
steps.note: PAGER=cat is a temporary environment-variable assignment for one command; it does not permanently change your shell or Ansible configuration. Omit it when you prefer paged output in a normal terminal.
steps.troubleshooting: If ansible-doc cannot find the module, confirm ansible-core is installed and that the Ansible executable and Python environment come from the expected RHEL package.

steps.label: Test
steps.title: Run a functional smoke test
steps.alt: Ansible localhost ping module returning a successful pong response
steps.explanation: This is an Ansible ad hoc command: ansible starts the CLI, localhost is the target host pattern, -m selects a module, and ansible.builtin.ping is the fully qualified module name. The -c local option uses Ansible's local connection instead of SSH, so the module runs on this control node without an inventory or remote host. Unlike the operating-system ping utility, this module does not send ICMP packets; it verifies that Ansible can execute Python and return JSON successfully.
steps.expected: localhost returns SUCCESS with ping: pong and changed: false.
steps.note: You now have a working Ansible control node and can continue with inventories, playbooks, and collections.
steps.troubleshooting: An implicit-inventory warning can be normal for this localhost-only test. The important result is localhost | SUCCESS and ping: pong.

troubleshooting.title: rhc connect cannot register the system
troubleshooting.detail: Confirm internet access, DNS resolution, an accurate system clock, and any required proxy configuration. Verify that the Red Hat account has an active RHEL entitlement, then retry rhc connect.

troubleshooting.title: BaseOS or AppStream is not enabled
troubleshooting.command:
sudo subscription-manager refresh
sudo subscription-manager repos \
  --enable="rhel-9-for-$(arch)-baseos-rpms" \
  --enable="rhel-9-for-$(arch)-appstream-rpms"
troubleshooting.detail: Refresh the entitlement data and enable the repository IDs that match the system architecture. Run dnf repolist --enabled again to confirm both repositories.

troubleshooting.title: DNF reports: No match for argument ansible-core
troubleshooting.command:
sudo dnf clean all
sudo dnf makecache
sudo dnf repoquery --latest-limit 1 ansible-core
troubleshooting.detail: This usually means AppStream is unavailable or the local metadata is stale. Rebuild the cache only after confirming the repository is enabled.

troubleshooting.title: The localhost smoke test shows a warning
troubleshooting.detail: A warning about the implicit localhost or an empty inventory is expected in this inventory-free test. Continue if the result contains SUCCESS and ping: pong.

completion: rhc status reports active Subscription Management and Insights connections
rpm -q ansible-core returns the installed package
rpm -V ansible-core reports no package-file differences
ansible-config and ansible-doc return usable output
The localhost ping test returns SUCCESS and ping: pong

cleanup.explanation: Cleanup is optional. Remove the package only if this VM will not be used for later Ansible labs. Unregistering also removes access to subscribed RHEL content.
cleanup.command:
sudo dnf remove ansible-core
# Optional: disconnect this disposable lab VM
sudo rhc disconnect
